Posted March 8, 2000
(MarijuanaNews note: Marijuana arrests soared under Clinton, and the suppression of medical marijuana became the state ideology. Why? I think that there is substantial evidence that Clinton has long been vulnerable to blackmail by the DEA and others who knew about his involvement in hard drug smuggling through Arkansas when he was governor. This book gives an insight into this wretched business.)

The Boys on the Tracks by Mara Leveritt
Hardcover - 384 pages (November 1999) VHPS/St. Martins Press; ISBN: 0312198418
Reviewed By Stephen Young http://home.att.net/~theyoungfamily
(MarijuanaNews note: Steve Young is a reader of MarijuanaNews, and I appreciate his sending me this review.)

Corruption feeds on the drug war. It should be obvious to anyone following reports about Los Angeles Police officers who brutalized and framed suspects. The negative influence of the drug war on police has been well documented, but the damage drug prohibition does to other areas of government hasn't been explored as carefully.

Arkansas journalist Mara Leveritt helps to remedy that situation with her great book The Boys on the Tracks. Leveritt has been a vocal supporter of medical marijuana in Arkansas (see http://marijuananews.com/news.php3?sid=115), but this work tackles another important aspect of prohibition.

The book shouldn't be judged by its cover. Subtitled " Death, Denial and a Mothers Crusade to Bring Her Son's Killers to Justice, " it doesn't at first appear to be a careful examination of drug-related corruption. But it is, and it shows how officials and institutions at the local, state and federal level are affected

The boys on the tracks are a pair of teenagers who died, allegedly, after being run over by a train. The state medical examiner of Arkansas determined the boys had died because they were intoxicated with marijuana, so intoxicated that they did not notice a speeding locomotive was about to crush them. Many people found this explanation unbelievable, particularly the parents of the boys. However, the parents' attempts to find out how the
boys were killed before the train hit them were rebuffed by government officials at every level.

The mother of one of the boys dedicated herself to finding out what really happened. While she doesn't get a definitive answer by the book's end, she learns just how deeply drug corruption has tainted the public officials she thought she could trust. As it becomes clear that her son's killing had more to do with the violent market for hard drugs than any personal drug use, the mother learns that some parts of that black market are carefully
protected by authorities. And that the black market isn't merely a local phenomena; it seems to be related to an international drug ring operating without interference from the FBI, CIA or anyone else.

The huge money and wild emotions surrounding the illegal drug market certainly made many of the astonishing incidents in the book possible. The author does a good job putting a human face on the victims of corruption as well as the corrupted officials themselves. One figure in the book, an elected prosecutor, serves as an emblem for officials who understand the power of illegal drug markets - and methods to harness that power. Illegal drugs seemed to be the prosecutor's link between the " legitimate " world of the law, the more shadowy world of politics, and the underworld of crime.

The prosecutor used anti-drug law to help his allies and hurt his enemies.

He certainly took personal pleasure and profit from illegal drugs, but he built a reputation of being anti-drug crusader. He even exploited fears about drug war infringements on personal rights when he was jailed for refusing to take a court-mandated drug test.

The whole story could be used as a symbol for the smokescreen created by the war on drugs. The boys' deaths were officially blamed on marijuana, the all purpose scapegoat, while the black market for hard drugs seems to be the real cause for their killings.

" The Boys on the Tracks " doesn't explore drug policy explicitly, but the story illustrates, from a fresh angle, how much damage our current drug policy can do. Many people seem to think that if they avoid illegal drugs, they won't be affected by the drug war. This book, in a very readable and entertaining manner, shows how naive that position is. I recommend it to reformers, but also to skeptics who still think the drug war is someone else's problem.

Excerpt From Kirkus Reviews


" Award-winning investigative reporter Leveritt’s debut is a wrecking-ball tale of tragedy, malfeasance, and machine politics that resembles an all-true Arkansas Confidential. In 1987, Linda Ives suffered a parental worst-nightmare when her son and a friend were run over by a train, whose crew observed them supine and covered with a tarp before impact. Local law enforcement attributed the deaths to a massive overdose of marijuana and dismissed the crews tale as optical illusion, in the first of many suspicious official fumbles.

Ives compelled a series of investigations that began promisingly yet were inexplicably stifled by such malign forces as the states notoriously incompetent medical examiner (protected by then-Governor Clinton) and an admired local prosecutor who championed her cause as camouflage for his own criminal activities. As years passed, and more unsolved killings occurred, Ives assembled evidence that the boys had stumbled upon a diffuse conspiracy involving CIA-backed air suppliers to the Contras, who ran an enormous cocaine-trafficking operation from a remote airport.

Fanciful as this may sound, Leveritt documents how Ives’ quest for transparency was consistently stymied, first by local agencies, then the state police, finally by the FBI. A portrait emerges of state governance as a deeply corrupted good-ol'-boy network, funded by drug money and protected by blackmail and violence. "
